title: Frontier AI Safety Standards Working Session
summary: Rare joint working session ahead of the Commerce briefing, brokered by both labs' policy teams. Despite ongoing litigation between the companies, the two agreed on a joint industry proposal: shared pre-deployment evaluation standards for frontier models built on both labs' internal eval suites, a confidential cross-lab incident-reporting channel with 72-hour disclosure for critical findings, and support for a compute-threshold-based definition of frontier models. They explicitly did not agree on chip export policy or open-weights policy and will argue those separately at the briefing.
decisions: Jointly propose shared pre-deployment evaluation standards for bio, cyber, and autonomy risks at the Commerce briefing
Stand up a confidential cross-lab incident-reporting channel with 72-hour disclosure for critical safety findings
Support defining frontier models by training-compute threshold, reviewed annually
Chip export policy and open-weights policy are explicitly excluded; each lab argues its own position
The litigation stays fully out of the joint proposal; policy teams work through counsel-approved channels

action_items.task: Send the merged eval-suite draft combining both labs' pre-deployment protocols to the joint policy team
Deliver xAI's incident-taxonomy draft and the 72-hour disclosure trigger definitions
Invite the other frontier labs to co-sign the proposal before the Commerce briefing

transcript.speaker: Sam Altman
transcript.text: Elon. So our policy teams conspired to put us in a room. I was told there would be no lawyers present, which for us is practically a novelty act at this point.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: The lawyers are billing either way, Sam, they don't need to be in the room to be present in spirit. Let's stipulate the obvious up front: we're suing each other, I think your corporate structure went somewhere it shouldn't have, you think I'm — I've read what you think. None of that is today. Today is the narrow thing.

transcript.speaker: Sam Altman
transcript.text: Agreed, and let me say the narrow thing precisely, because it's the only way this meeting works. In four weeks Commerce holds a briefing that will shape frontier AI regulation for years. If the labs show up divided on everything, we get rules written by whoever lobbies last — you saw the chip thing nearly get decided by meeting order. There's a small set of things you and I actually agree on, and if the two loudest people in AI co-sign them, they probably become the standard. That's the entire agenda.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: That's the agenda I came for. Here's my list of where I think we genuinely overlap, tell me where I'm wrong. One: pre-deployment evals for catastrophic risk — bio, cyber, autonomous replication — should be standardized and mandatory at the frontier, not voluntary blog posts. Two: when a lab finds something scary, other labs should hear about it before the press does. Three: 'frontier' should be defined by training compute, because it's the only thing you can actually measure from outside.

transcript.speaker: Sam Altman
transcript.text: You're not wrong on any of the three, which I find genuinely annoying. On evals — we've published our preparedness framework, you've published your risk thresholds, and anyone who reads both carefully can see they're eighty percent the same document wearing different clothes. My proposal: our teams merge them into one shared pre-deployment suite for the catastrophic categories. Not the capability benchmarks, not the product evals — just the 'should this thing exist in public' tests. I'll have a merged draft to the joint team by the 18th.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: Agreed, with one condition that matters to me: the eval suite gets versioned publicly, even if the results per model stay confidential. The public should be able to read what we test for, so 'passed the evals' means something checkable rather than being pure vibes. Otherwise we've just built a nicer-looking rubber stamp.

transcript.speaker: Sam Altman
transcript.text: Public suite, confidential per-model results — I can live with that, and honestly it protects us both the first time either of us has to delay a launch. Which brings me to incident reporting, and here I want to be more concrete than the usual polite version. Twice in the last year we've found jailbreak classes during red-teaming that almost certainly work on your models too. There is currently no non-awkward way for my team to tell your team. The current channel is, functionally, Twitter.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: The current channel being my own platform is very funny and also a real indictment. Same story from our side — the Grok team found a fine-tuning attack in February that we sat on for three weeks because legal couldn't figure out how to disclose it to a company we're actively suing without it becoming a discovery issue. Three weeks is unacceptable for something in that category. So: confidential cross-lab channel, security-cleared staff only, seventy-two-hour disclosure clock for critical findings, and — this is the important part — a litigation firewall. Nothing in the channel is admissible or discoverable in any dispute between member labs. Counsel-approved, so it actually survives contact with our respective legal departments.

transcript.speaker: Sam Altman
transcript.text: The litigation firewall is the unlock, yes — that's the clause that makes it real instead of aspirational. Seventy-two hours for critical is right. I'd add a severity taxonomy so 'critical' isn't self-graded into meaninglessness; you know as well as I do that every lab's instinct is to call its own incidents 'moderate.'

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: We'll draft the taxonomy — xAI's incident classification is the thing I'd actually hold up against anyone's, and I'll send it with the disclosure trigger definitions by the 18th so both drafts land together. Okay, compute thresholds. This one's easy for me: define frontier by training FLOPs, reviewed annually because the number decays, and regulation attaches at the threshold. It's imperfect but it's objective, and every alternative — capability-based definitions, model-card self-declaration — collapses into labs grading themselves.

transcript.speaker: Sam Altman
transcript.text: Agreed, with the annual review being load-bearing — a fixed threshold written in 2026 becomes either meaningless or strangling by 2028, and I genuinely don't know which, which is exactly why it has to be reviewed. Fine. So that's three real agreements. Now let's be equally precise about the disagreements, because if we blur them the whole proposal loses credibility. Chips: you want the frontier tier export-restricted, I think that's directionally right but you'd draw the line tighter than me. And open weights: you've released weights of older models and think it's fine; I think the frontier-minus-one generation is exactly the layer where it starts being dangerous.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: Correct on both, and my position is those fights make the joint proposal stronger, not weaker — two people who are suing each other and disagree about half of policy still co-signing these three things is precisely what makes the three things credible. We put a scope clause at the top: this proposal covers evals, incident reporting, and thresholds. Full stop. Chips and open weights, we each show up at Commerce and argue our own book, ideally back to back for maximum theater.

transcript.speaker: Sam Altman
transcript.text: The scope clause is right. And we should get the other labs on it before the briefing — this lands very differently as an industry letter than as 'the two exes agree on custody terms.' I'll make the calls; the labs will take the meeting faster if it comes from me, no offense intended, some offense probably unavoidable.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: Offense noted and survivable — you make the calls, you're better at the diplomatic circuit and I have five Starships to launch. Last thing, and I want an honest answer rather than a press answer. The timelines we're both running at — does the pace scare you? Actually scare you?

transcript.speaker: Sam Altman
transcript.text: Honest answer: yes, on maybe one day in ten, and the other nine days I think we're building the most important tool humanity has ever had and the pace is the point. The ratio used to be one in thirty. That shift is why I'm in this room with you despite everything — the disagreement between us was never about whether this needs guardrails. It was about who could be trusted to hold them.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: One in ten is about my number too, and the honest overlap is why this meeting worked. For the record, Sam — I still think I'm right about the structure, you still think you're right about me, and the courts will disappoint us both at extraordinary hourly rates. But the evals, the channel, the thresholds — that part we just did in fifty minutes. Should have done it two years ago.

transcript.speaker: Sam Altman
transcript.text: Two years ago neither of us would have taken the meeting. Drafts exchanged on the 18th, other labs invited by the 25th, joint proposal filed before the briefing. And Elon — good luck in November. I mean that without a single caveat, which may be a first for us.
